danish.title: Trettende bog (1812) — Kapitel 17
paragraphs: Kutuzov sov som alle gamle mennesker ikke meget om natten. Han faldt ofte uventet i søvn om dagen, men om natten lå han som regel vågen på sin seng uden at klæde sig af, tænkende.
Sådan lå han nu på sin seng og støttede sit store, tunge, arrede hoved på sin fyldige hånd med det ene øje åbent, grublende og stirrende ind i mørket.

Siden Bennigsen, der korresponderede med kejseren og havde mere indflydelse end nogen anden i staben, var begyndt at undgå ham, var Kutuzov mere rolig med hensyn til muligheden for, at han og hans tropper ville blive tvunget til at deltage i nytteløse offensive bevægelser. Lektionen fra slaget ved Tarutino og dagen forinden, som Kutuzov mindedes med smerte, måtte, tænkte han, også have en vis virkning på andre.

"De må forstå, at vi kun kan tabe ved at gå til angreb. Tålmodighed og tid er mine krigere, mine stridsmænd," tænkte Kutuzov. Han vidste, at man ikke bør plukke et æble, mens det er grønt. Det falder af sig selv, når det er modent, men plukkes det umodent, ødelægges æblet, træet skades, og man får gåsehud på tænderne. Som en erfaren jæger vidste han, at dyret var såret, og såret som kun hele Ruslands styrke kunne have såret det, men om det var dødeligt såret eller ej, var stadig et uafgjort spørgsmål. Nu, ud fra det faktum at Lauriston og Barthélemi var blevet sendt, og ud fra guerillastyrkernes rapporter, var Kutuzov næsten sikker på, at såret var dødeligt. Men han manglede yderligere beviser og måtte vente.

"De vil løbe hen og se, hvor hårdt de har såret det. Vent, så skal vi se! Uophørlige manøvrer, uophørlige fremryk!" tænkte han. "Hvad for? Kun for at udmærke sig! Som om krig var en leg. De er som børn, man ikke kan få en fornuftig forklaring ud af, fordi de alle vil vise, hvor godt de kan slås. Men det er ikke det, der er brug for nu.

"Og sikke snedige manøvrer, de alle foreslår mig! Det forekommer dem, at når de har udtænkt to-tre muligheder" — han mindedes den generelle plan, der var sendt ham fra Petersborg — "har de forudset alt. Men mulighederne er uendelige."

Det uafgjorte spørgsmål om, hvorvidt det sår, der var tilføjet ved Borodino, var dødeligt eller ej, havde hængt over Kutuzovs hoved i en hel måned. På den ene side havde franskmændene besat Moskva. På den anden side var Kutuzov med hele sit væsen overbevist om, at det forfærdelige slag, hvori han og alle russere havde lagt al deres kraft, måtte have været dødeligt. Men under alle omstændigheder var der brug for beviser; han havde ventet en hel måned på dem og blev mere utålmodig, jo længere han ventede. I sine søvnløse nætter gjorde han netop det, han bebrejdede de yngre generaler for at gøre. Han forestillede sig alle mulige udfald, ligesom de yngre mænd, men med den forskel, at han så tusinder af muligheder i stedet for to-tre og ikke baserede noget på dem. Jo længere han tænkte, jo flere muligheder viste sig. Han forestillede sig alle slags bevægelser af Napoleons hær, som helhed eller i dele — mod Petersborg, mod ham selv, for at omgå ham. Han tænkte også på muligheden (som han frygtede mest af alt) for, at Napoleon ville kæmpe mod ham med hans eget våben og forblive i Moskva og afvente ham. Kutuzov forestillede sig endda, at Napoleons hær kunne vende tilbage via Medyn og Jukhnov, men det eneste, han ikke kunne forudse, var det, der skete — den sindssyge, krampagtige flugt af Napoleons hær i de første elleve dage efter afmarschen fra Moskva: en flugt, der muliggjorde det, Kutuzov endnu ikke havde turdet tænke på — den fuldstændige tilintetgørelse af den franske hær. Dorokhovs rapport om Broussiers division, guerillastyrkernes meldinger om nøden i Napoleons hær og rygterne om forberedelser til at forlade Moskva bekræftede alle formodningen om, at den franske hær var slået og forberedte sig på flugt. Men det var blot formodninger, som syntes vigtige for de yngre mænd, men ikke for Kutuzov. Med sine tres års erfaring vidste han, hvad rygter var værd, vidste, hvor tilbøjelige mennesker, der ønsker noget, er til at gruppere alle nyheder, så de bekræfter det ønskede, og vidste, hvor let de i sådanne tilfælde ser bort fra alt, der taler imod. Og jo mere han ønskede det, jo mindre tillod han sig at tro det. Dette spørgsmål opslugte al hans åndskapacitet. Alt andet var blot livets vanlige rutine. Til denne rutine hørte hans samtaler med staben, de breve, han skrev fra Tarutino til Madame de Staël, romanlæsning, tildeling af udmærkelser, hans korrespondance med Petersborg og så videre. Men tilintetgørelsen af franskmændene, som han alene forudså, var hans hjertes eneste ønske.
Natten den ellevte oktober lå han på sin arm og tænkte på det.
Der var uro i det tilstødende værelse, og han hørte Tolls, Konovnitsyns og Bolkhovitinovs skridt.
"Nå, hvem er der? Kom ind, kom ind! Hvad nyt?" kaldte feltmarskalken til dem.
Mens en tjener tændte et lys, meddelte Toll substansen af nyheden.
"Hvem bragte den?" spurgte Kutuzov med et blik, der, da lyset blev tændt, slog Toll ved sin kolde strenghed.
"Der kan ikke være tvivl, Deres højhed."
"Kald ham ind, kald ham herind."

Kutuzov satte sig op med det ene ben dinglende ned fra sengen og sin store mave hvilende mod det andet, der var trukket op under ham. Han kneb det seende øje sammen for at granske budbringeren nøjere, som om han ønskede at læse i hans ansigt det, der optog hans eget sind.

"Fortæl mig, fortæl mig, min ven," sagde han til Bolkhovitiov med sin lave, aldrende stemme, mens han trak den skjorte sammen, der stod åben på hans bryst, "kom nærmere — nærmere. Hvilke nyheder bringer du mig? Hm? At Napoleon har forladt Moskva? Er du sikker? Hm?"
Bolkhovitiov gav en detaljeret beretning fra begyndelsen af alt, hvad han var blevet bedt om at rapportere.
"Tal hurtigere, hurtigere! Pin mig ikke!" afbrød Kutuzov ham.

Bolkhovitiov fortalte ham alt og tav så i forventning om instrukser. Toll var ved at sige noget, men Kutuzov standsede ham. Han forsøgte at sige noget, men hans ansigt rynkede sig pludseligt og forvrængedes; han vinkede Toll væk med hånden og vendte sig mod den modsatte side af værelset, mod det hjørne, der lå i halvmørke af ikonerne, som hang der.
"Åh Herre, min skaber, Du har hørt vor bøn..." sagde han med skælvende stemme og foldede hænder. "Rusland er frelst. Jeg takker Dig, Herre!" og han græd.

english.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: Kutuzov, like all old people, slept very little at night. He often dropped off unexpectedly during the day, but at night, lying on his bed fully clothed, he generally stayed awake thinking.
So he lay now on his bed, resting his large, heavy, scarred head on his plump hand, with his one good eye open, pondering and peering into the darkness.

Since Bennigsen—who corresponded with the Emperor and held more influence than anyone else on the staff—had begun avoiding him, Kutuzov felt more at ease about the possibility of himself and his troops being forced into useless offensive operations. The lesson of the Battle of Tarutino and the day before it, which Kutuzov remembered with pain, must, he thought, have some effect on others too.

'They must understand that we can only lose by attacking. Patience and time are my warriors, my champions,' thought Kutuzov. He knew that you shouldn't pick an apple while it's still green. It will fall by itself when ripe. But if you pick it unripe, you ruin the apple, damage the tree, and set your teeth on edge. Like an experienced hunter, he knew the beast was wounded—wounded as only the combined strength of Russia could have wounded it. But whether the wound was mortal remained an open question. Now, from the fact that Lauriston and Barthélemi had been sent, and from the guerrillas' reports, Kutuzov was almost sure the wound was fatal. But he needed more proof, and he had to wait.

'They want to run over and see how badly they've hurt it. Wait, and we'll see! All these maneuvers, all these advances!' he thought. 'What for? Only to make themselves look good. As if fighting were some kind of game. They're like children who can't give you a sensible account of what happened because they all want to show how well they can fight. But that's not what's needed now.'

'And what elaborate maneuvers they all propose to me! They seem to think that when they've considered two or three possibilities'—he recalled the general plan sent from Petersburg—'they've thought of everything. But the possibilities are endless.'

The unresolved question of whether the wound inflicted at Borodino was mortal had hung over Kutuzov's head for an entire month. On the one hand, the French had occupied Moscow. On the other, Kutuzov felt certain with his whole being that the terrible blow into which he and all of Russia had poured their strength must have been fatal. But he needed proof. He had waited a whole month and was growing more impatient every day. Lying on his bed during those sleepless nights, he did exactly what he criticized the younger generals for doing: he imagined every possible scenario. But unlike them, he saw thousands of possibilities instead of two or three, and based nothing on any of them. He imagined every conceivable movement of Napoleon's army—as a whole or in parts—against Petersburg, or against him, or to outflank him. He also considered the possibility he feared most: that Napoleon might turn his own weapon against him and simply stay in Moscow, waiting him out. Kutuzov even imagined the French army turning back through Medyn and Yukhnov. But the one thing he could not foresee was what actually happened: the insane, convulsive stampede of Napoleon's army during its first eleven days after leaving Moscow—a stampede that made possible what Kutuzov hadn't yet dared to imagine: the complete destruction of the French. Dorokhov's report about Broussier's division, the guerrillas' reports of distress in Napoleon's army, and rumors of preparations to leave Moscow all supported the idea that the French army was beaten and preparing to flee. But these were only suppositions, which seemed important to the younger men but not to Kutuzov. With his sixty years of experience, he knew the value of rumors, knew how readily people who want something will arrange all the news to confirm their wishes, and ignore everything that contradicts them. The more he wanted to believe, the less he allowed himself to. This question consumed all his mental energy. Everything else was mere routine—his conversations with the staff, his letters to Madame de Staël, his reading of novels, the distribution of awards, his correspondence with Petersburg, and so on. But the destruction of the French, which he alone foresaw, was his heart's one desire.
On the night of the eleventh of October, he lay propped on his arm, thinking about it.
There was movement in the next room, and he heard the footsteps of Toll, Konovnitsyn, and Bolkhovitinov.
'Hello—who's there? Come in, come in! What news?' the field marshal called out.
While a servant lit a candle, Toll communicated the substance of the news.
'Who brought it?' asked Kutuzov, and when the candle was lit, Toll was struck by the cold severity of his expression.
'There can be no doubt about it, Your Highness.'
'Call him in. Bring him here.'

Kutuzov sat up with one leg hanging off the bed and his large belly resting against the other leg, which was doubled under him. He squinted his seeing eye to scrutinize the messenger more carefully, as if trying to read in his face what occupied his own mind.

'Tell me, tell me, my friend,' he said to Bolkhovitinov in his low, aged voice, pulling together the shirt that gaped open on his chest. 'Come closer—closer. What news have you brought? Napoleon has left Moscow? Are you sure?'
Bolkhovitinov gave a detailed account of everything he had been told to report.
'Speak faster, faster! Don't torture me!' Kutuzov interrupted.

Bolkhovitinov told him everything and fell silent, awaiting orders. Toll started to say something, but Kutuzov stopped him. He tried to speak himself, but his face suddenly crumpled and wrinkled. He waved his arm at Toll and turned to the opposite side of the room, toward the corner darkened by the icons hanging there.
'O Lord, my Creator, You have heard our prayer...' he said in a trembling voice, with folded hands. 'Russia is saved. I thank You, O Lord!' And he wept.
